newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan awaits Beirut move on Red Army members.
newsitem.headline: Japan awaits Beirut move on Red Army members.

text.p: Japan on Wednesday appeared to accept that it could take years to extradite five top Japanese Red Army members from Lebanon to face trial for some of the boldest terrorist attacks of the past two decades.

Government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said Japanese officials had identified the five to Lebanese authorities who planned to take their own action against the group before deciding on when they could be extradited.
"At present, we have no idea as to when they would be handed over to us," Kajiyama told reporters.
"We must first see whether they violated Lebanese laws. Their extradition may come after passing several hurdles," he added.

The guerrillas include Kozo Okamoto, 49, convicted by Israel of the 1972 massacre at Tel Aviv's Lod airport, the group's top spokesman Masao Adachi, 57, and its senior liaison officer Mariko Yamamoto, 56.

The other two were Kazuo Tohira, 44, freed from prison by Japan in 1975 in exchange for hostages held when Red Army members stormed the U.S. Embassy in Kuala Lumpur, and Haruo Wako, 48, a former student activist who was the suspected leader of a Red Army commando unit.
Lebanese judicial sources had told Reuters in Beirut that one of the group was Hisashi Matsuda, 48.
But a spokesman for Japan's National Police Agency said this was a mistake and Wako was in custody in Beirut, not Matsuda.
Japan has been trying to negotiate an early extradition of the five extreme leftists, who were all on international wanted lists.

But Japanese government sources said they now believed it could take up to two years before Lebanon returned the high-profile guerrillas to Tokyo because they could first be tried in Beirut on charges of carrying forged passports.
Lebanon and Japan do not have an extradition treaty.
The sources said Japan was handling the affair carefully to avoid repercussions on the present hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
"Japan must show how serious we are about terrorist activities, including the hostage crisis in Peru," one source said.
Marxist rebels seized the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima in December, taking hundreds of people hostage. They still hold 72 captives.
Intelligence sources say the Red Army, which once numbered hundreds, has dwindled to about 40 middle-aged members who are scattered in hideouts around the world.

Apart from a series of hijacks and attacks on airports and embassies in the 1970s, some members of the Japanese Red Army, led by 51-year-old woman Fusako Shigenobu, are suspected of torturing and killing a dozen comrades who threatened to inform on them in Japan.
The Red Army, founded in 1971, is allied to hardline anti-Israeli Palestinian factions.
Japanese police believe Red Army members ran a guerrilla training camp in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley which was a haven during Lebanon's 1975-90 civil war.
